summary: This RFC specifies a Telnet option for exchanging terminal type information. It supersedes RFC 884, with the one change that the TERMINAL-TYPE IS sub-negotiation is sent only in answer to a SEND request. It was replaced by RFC 1091.

plainLanguage.summary: The Telnet TERMINAL-TYPE option lets one host ask the other for its terminal's name. RFC 930 requires the name to be sent only after a SEND request, and was later replaced by RFC 1091.

subtitle: A Telnet option for requesting a name for the connected terminal

tldr.problem: A Telnet server may need to know the kind of terminal connected to a user program.
tldr.mechanism: The peers negotiate the TERMINAL-TYPE option, then the requester sends SEND and the other peer replies with IS and a terminal name.
tldr.outcome: RFC 930 superseded RFC 884 and was later replaced by RFC 1091.

sections.title: Why Exchange a Terminal Name
sections.content:
The TERMINAL-TYPE option lets a Telnet server learn the type of terminal connected to a user's Telnet program. A process may use that information to tailor data to the terminal, including functions such as cursor addressing or multiple colors that are not part of the Network Virtual Terminal specification.

The option is numbered 24. By default, the peers do not exchange terminal type information unless they negotiate the option.
sections.plainLanguage: A Telnet host can ask what kind of terminal is connected. The answer may let a program choose display features that suit that terminal.

sections.title: Request and Reply
sections.content:
WILL and DO commands grant permission for later discussion; they do not carry the terminal name. Once the peers exchange WILL and DO for TERMINAL-TYPE, the sender of DO may send a SEND subcommand (code 1). The sender of WILL may answer with an IS subcommand (code 0) and the terminal name.

The name is an NVT ASCII string, with upper- and lower-case letters treated as equivalent. It may not be sent spontaneously: the IS reply must answer a SEND request.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosts first agree to exchange terminal information. One then asks with SEND, and the other replies with IS and a name; it must not send the name without being asked.

sections.title: Terminal Names and Alternatives
sections.content:
The RFC says the Assigned Numbers list maintains terminal names to reduce confusion from different spellings. A name may be any NVT ASCII string meaningful to both hosts, and its maximum length is 40 characters. UNKNOWN is used when the terminal type is unknown or unlikely to be recognized by the other party.

If a terminal has several names, the sender can provide them from most specific to least specific in response to successive SEND requests. The server should stop asking after receiving the same reply twice; the sender signals that it has no more names by repeating its last name.
sections.plainLanguage: A terminal name can be up to 40 characters. If a device has several names, it can offer them one at a time, and repeating a name signals that there are no more alternatives.
